keyVerseText: Notwithstanding thou mayest kill and eat flesh in all thy gates, whatsoever thy soul lusteth after, according to the blessing of the LORD thy God which he hath given thee: the unclean and the clean may eat thereof, as of the roebuck, and as of the hart.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun אַוָּה (ʼavvâh), derived from the root אָוָה (ʼâvâh), fundamentally conveys a sense of deep desire or longing. This root carries nuances of craving and coveting, often associated with both physical appetite and emotional yearning. Unlike the English term 'lust,' which frequently implies moral negativity, the root meaning here encompasses a broad spectrum of desire, including natural, morally neutral human longings as well as divine will. This etymological insight highlights that the word denotes an intense inward inclination or appetite, not inherently sinful but powerful and significant.
usageInScripture: Throughout its seven occurrences, אַוָּה consistently denotes a strong desire or pleasure, often translated as 'lusteth after' three times, but also rendered as 'with all the desire,' 'at her pleasure,' and 'It is in my desire.' This range of translations underscores the word's flexibility, capturing both human longing and divine disposition. It appears in contexts describing natural appetites, such as desire for meat, as well as spiritual or royal pleasure, indicating that the term encompasses both physical and metaphysical realms of wanting. The usage reveals that אַוָּה is a term for earnest longing that can be morally neutral or positively oriented, depending on context.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding אַוָּה enriches our grasp of biblical anthropology and divine-human interaction by recognizing desire as an integral part of God's creation rather than inherently sinful. The term's neutrality invites believers to discern between God-honoring desires and those that lead away from holiness. It reminds us that God himself expresses will and pleasure, aligning human longing with divine purpose when rightly ordered. This insight encourages a Christ-centered faith that embraces God-given desires as part of our nature, redeemed and fulfilled in relationship with Him. Recognizing the complexity of desire helps believers pursue holiness without denying the God-ordained impulses of the soul.
keyVerseReflection: Deuteronomy 12:15 states, 'whatsoever thy soul lusteth after,' using אַוָּה to describe the lawful desire for meat within the covenant community. Here, the word conveys a permitted and natural longing that God blesses, emphasizing that not all desires are forbidden but can be enjoyed according to divine blessing. The use of אַוָּה in this verse reassures believers that God acknowledges and provides for human desires in a way that honors His covenant, inviting a joyful and grateful approach to His provision.
